Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Howard R. Scott
Reel 1

Washington, D. C.
March 8, 1979

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

I don't know where I got my musical talent. Neither one of my parents was musically inclined or knew anything about music. But ever since I was a very small child, music always appealed to me. And I was told by my parents that when I was very, very small, whenever any music or big band passed or something, they couldn't control me, they couldn't hold me. I had to go, wanted to go where they were. I wanted to be with them.

It went on like that, my mother and father were very religious people. And they used to go to church every Sunday. So my father finally told my mother, said, maybe he's got something in him that's musically inclined. He said, I just heard that down at the church they're having a boys band they're forming, a children's band, and maybe he could get into that.

Mama said, well, take him down then and see. Well, I had got a pair of little wooden sticks, and I used to practice with the -- drumming all over everything, used to get a spanking every time I made a little noise. And I went down with my father and had my little wooden sticks with me. It was a boys band, but everybody in there wanted to be a drummer, said Professor Young. So we had too many drummers. They put me on a cornet. They needed cornets, they (unintelligible). Well, that was music.
When were you-- what was the --
I was nine years old at the time.
What is your correct date of birth?
1903? And the month and the day?
November 1.
So you were nine when they gave you a coronet.
Huh?
So you were nine when they gave you the coronet.

Oh, that was music. And he was very good, that Professor Young. He taught basic music. And I was eager to learn, and he said I was a good pupil. And I learned how to play coronet from him. Well, I went very religiously and regularly to the rehearsals, and I learned to play. And I used to practice at home. They let me play until they got tired and told me to stop that noise, and I had to stop.

Well, that was downtown. We slowly moved uptown. This is Manhattten, and I became acquainted with some older fellows, and a boys band was two young fellows. Willie and Lewis Dover, had a band. And I heard of it, and they had heard of me. So we got together. It was a nice little band, young fellows, very young. And we rehearsed together very religiously and all that kind of - we got work. At that time there wasn't very many people in New York, no cars and anything, and
they used to have a lot of block parties. We played for block parties at the end of the week, and my little extra money came in handy, to the family.
So I kept on with them, and from one little band to another, I made progress.
What sort of music were you playing?
Just the ordinary music at that time, like, popular music, mostly. And it was strictly jazz, because we weren't reading much. Although I had been taught to read.
Well, from then on, I joined another little band, and we started to play for little dances. Then I was reading music then. That was really nice, all right.

Well, war came in, and I was playing then, and working and playing and working and playing on the weekends, got a little job. I was still in school. Well, at school, I went to the High School of Commerce. They had an assembly band, orchestra, that is, then they had a band for the football and the baseball games, High School of Commerce, 66th Street off Broadway. They tore it down now, but they had a place there.

But, anyhow, I played in both bands. Well, I learned a lot from that. I mean, I played in both bands at the games that they played, and at the assemblies when the students were there. Well, one thing led to another. I was getting experience a lot, and I wanted it so badly. The fellows came from World War I, the soldiers came back. The colored regiment was

the 15th Regiment. And when they came, they marched on up Fifth Avenue on up to Harlem. I was down there to meet them. And (unintelligible) had the 15th band, don't you know, I walked all the way with that band on the sidewalk, all the way up to Harlem, and just listened to it. I was so inspired with it.

Well, it so happened that in playing around, I met one of the fellows that was in the band, by the name of Cecil Smith. He was a saxophone player. He became interested in me, I don't know why. He just liked me, that's all. And talking with fellows I'd met, musicians. And he asked me, hey, Scotty, what you doing? You working? I said, no. He says, do you belong (unintelligible)? I said, no. He said, well, that's right, you're too young.

I was still in high school. He said, can you work weekends? I said, oh, yes, sure, sure, sure. He said, well, I'll tell you, you have to come a long way, down on Long Island. He says, but I'll take you out there. He had heard me play, and he said, I could do all right. This fellow was named Honey Potter of Freeport, Long Island. If Honey Potter had been a businessman and had a good education, he could have made a million dollars. He had most of the work out there in Long Island.
See, everything was live music then. There was no radio, and no -- of course, no television. Well, we used to go from Harlem and drive out to Long Island. Honey's wife --

he had a nice house on Bennington Avenue, and his wife, Nellie, she used to cook for us and we'd eat a meal, then we'd drive to where we'd be playing. Mostly it was firemen and policemen's balls. Those people (unintelligible). And, well, it was -- I enjoyed every minute of it.
Honey, he could only play in certain keys, but I knew those keys, and right away, they liked me. So every weekend, there it went, Honey Potter, Honey Potter, Honey Potter.
What did Honey play?

He played piano. He's a pianist. And he read by ear. But by then, of course, I finally had got a Victrola, and records. And, of course, I got all the records I could get and listened to them, and I had a quick ear. When I'd hear a band playing a number, I had it. That tune was in there, see.

So on the job, if they got a new number to play, I knew it. They'd all say, hey, Scottie, where did you get that? How do you know this number? I wouldn't tell them. I said, I heard it, you know, like that. We lived uptown then, 131st Street, and 135th Street there was Lehmann's Music Shop. Well, to get all the accessories like mutes for my trumpet, and like that, I stopped there instead of having to go downtown.
I made friends with the old man Lehmann, the place is still there now, but it's mostly a card shop. The old man is dead, and his sons took over. He knew I was a musician, because
most of the time I was in a tuxedo. I used to come from high school, change my clothes, put on a tuxedo and then meet the fellows at the Amsterdam.

And we'd go out there. Well, they saw me there and they knew I was a musician. So all the records that came -- the new records from the shows and things, Mr. Lehmann used to save them for me. I'd take them home, play them on the record. Get my horn out, I had it, see. When I went to work, I had that number before those fellows got the music sheets. I knew it. So when they played it, I was able to take my solo.

Well, well, well, I got another job -- I couldn't join the Amsterdam, I was too young. But I met all those old fellows, and most of them had been in World War I. And they used to call me Kid Scottie at that time. Well, I didn't mind, I was so happy to be playing music with them. And I got a lot of experience from them, and all like that.

So finally, after playing around here, there and everywhere, I got a call one night. And a fellow said -- asked me who I was and I told him, and he said he was Fletcher Henderson. Well, I had heard something -- it wasn't many musicians in New York that -- anyone new comes to town, it just circulates very fast and the next day everybody knew there was a new guy in town.
And I had heard that a guy named Fletcher Henderson had -- but I didn't know nothing about him and all like that.
And he said he'd heard about me and he'd like for me to join his band.

Well, this Cecil Smith, I was still working with him, the same fellow. We were playing out at Honey Potter's, and I told him that I was working nights. And he said, that's all right, I'll see you the next day. So when I went out -- we went out there, I got Cecil to (unintelligible). I said, Cecil, I got to break the news to Honey Potter. Fletcher Henderson called me up and said he wanted me to join his band. Cecil said, that's great, Scotty, he says, but don't tell Honey now. Wait til you get through.

Well, when I went on that job that night, I played -- they told me I played like I never played before. I was so happy, in a way. And Cecil told me, he says, now, this is your big chance, Scottie, so you might as well take it. So after he got through, we worked on the North Side and we had to come to Hempstead to catch the 1:30 train. That was the only train coming into Penn Station at that time, before 7:00 in the morning.

So we got to the station. Honey drove us there and we went upstairs. Then I called Honey aside and told him. He was furious. He said, he'd knock every tooth out of my mouth before he'd let me go away. And the train came in to Dalton, and I was trying to plead with him. Cecil took me and pushed me in the train and the door closed. And he pushed me and he
kind of did like that to me. I said, you hurt me, Cecil, you hurt me. He says, you can't fight Honey. Honey is big and strong. Honey didn't want to let me go.

Well, they liked me over on the Island and I liked the different people. We played so many places, all over, all around. Even way out near Southampton and all that way. And, well, I joined Fletcher. Cecil told me he had a chance, Fletcher had talked to him, but he didn't want to take it. After all, he was older than me, much older. But he'd just came out of the Army and all like that, but that was my big chance.
Well, I joined Fletcher.
Now, wasn't this a new Fletcher Henderson band? He was forming a new band. It wasn't a band that you just joined. Didn't he form a band just to go into the Club Alabam?

No, well, I haven't come to that. I joined Fletcher. Well, we met, and he played at the Cotton Club. We played there a couple of weeks. Then we played at the . Then we played at the Lafayette Theatre, because that was the theatre in Harlem. We played at Lafayette Theatre, white people used to come there, too, and agents and things to see you. If you're good, you're booked downtown at the Palace Theatre. That was the big place, the Palace.
Well, they -- we played there, and then Fletcher told us that we were going to open up at 44th Street, off Broadway,

the Club Alabam.
Well, I was sailing on a cloud then. I was with a band, and those guys, they're all such good musicians. And to be able to play with them meant so much to me. I felt so great. Boy. That Coleman Hawkins, he was wonderful, marvelous. And Don Redman, he could play trumpet. He played all the reed instruments, and he played trumpet, too.

But the thing was, Fletcher was an arranger. He arranged all the music we played. We didn't play for the sheets. We played his arrangements. That's the thing that put his band -- made it a little different from the other bands, because they played from their music sheets. -- I.E., stock was.
(Inaudible.)

Yeah. Well, it got around, began getting around, Fletcher's name began to go up and everybody came to hear Fletcher, Fletcher, Fletcher, Fletcher. Then he wanted to expand his band. He wanted to get two more men. And he told us he was trying to get another trumpet player. That was Louis Armstrong, from -- he was out there in Chicago with Joe Oliver, the old man, Joe Oliver.

Well, we finally got Louis and he came to the band. He had high shoes on, button shoes. And a cardboard suitcase, and his stomach was way out like this. And they'd never been to New York before, and naturally, Broadway -- (unintelligible). But Alma and me, because we were the other trumpet players, we

took them in our hands, to ease his mind, and everything, and make him feel at home. Alma was a swell guy, too. He played trumpet, I played second and Louis was third, and took solos. See, I'd taken solos myself, but when Louis started to play -- whew, that was it.

Nothing like that had been heard before in New York, nothing like the way Louis played. He brought that New Orleans stuff here, and he played just a couple of nights there, and we left there. We had to open at Roseland. That's 51st Street and Broadway. That took up the whole block there. They had two bands there, one white and a big colored band.

Louis played that opening night at Roseland, and my goodness, people stopped dancing to come around and listen to him. He was scared at first. He said, how am I doing, Scottie? I said, listen, what I said, just close your eyes and play what you feel in your heart, in your body, in your mind. Just let it go, Louis, be yourself, that's all. Forget about the people. So he did. And they could hear him out in the street. And we were told that there were some people passing by that stopped, listening to him. He was so loud.

But he played. Well, that was the first night. The next night, you couldn't get in the place. Just that quick. It had gone all around about this new trumpet player at Roseland. Well, we had a great time there, we had a great time. We had a great time.
He couldn't read then, could he?
Hm?
Could Louis read?

Oh, yeah, he could -- well, he could read, but -- you know what I mean, Fletcher had arranged the music so that he wasn't obliged to read much. And mostly you relied on his trumpet solos. Louis could read, but he wasn't what you would call a topnotch reader. He could read a little, yeah. But what he had been playing mostly was just by ear. He could read a little.
Had you heard any recordings by him before then, before he came?
No, I had not heard any. In fact, I hadn't heard about Louis at all. But after he arrived here, then you began to hear everything, yes, indeed. Louis was a great guy.

Well, Duke came to town. And he was playing at the Kentucky Club, 48th Street and Broadway. Now, you know, in those days, it wasn't so many musicians, and Fletcher's band was the top band. And Paul Whitman had been named just a couple of years ago the King of Jazz. He was a violinist. And Paul Whitman came himself to hear Fletcher's band, and he said, if Fletcher was a white man, he would be a millionaire. That's just what he said. I heard him.
Well, Fletcher went up and up and up and up and up.

But he was a very strict leader. Every night, you had to stand up and stand inspection. He'd look at your hair, your face, see if you shaved, your shoes, see if they're shined. You had to be perfect to suit him. Of course, poor Louis, he was just the opposite when he joined the band, but all his faults and everything, his deficiencies, he made up in his playing. That -- nobody else could beat him playing at that time.

So we gradually got Louis -- oh, I'm a little ahead of my story. He had a cornet. Now, cornet is for a band, that was playing shrill. A trumpet is more mellow. Elmer and I took him downtown one day, we met him because Fletcher was beginning to play about Louis blowing so loud. He only had a cornet. We took him downtown, and we got him a trumpet. Well, he didn't know where to go, and we went down and got him a trumpet.

Well, he adjusted to that right away, because he had music in him. It was just a different horn, that was all. And so that made the band a little more even, three trumpets. So we continued and continued. In the meantime, there were rumors going around about Duke. Well, I didn't know what they meant and everything. And Fletcher -- oh, Louis came first. I was so busy talking about Louis I forgot about Buster.
Buster got there in time to open up in Roseland, so we had a full band then. Before that, it had just been Don Readman and Coleman Hawkins. Now, that made a trio then, and he
was excellent on that clarinet. Well, musicians came from far and wide just to see his band. But Duke was coming up, slowly but surely.
This is Duke.
Duke Ellington.
He had taken over the band from (inaudible) at that point.
No, he had his own band. He had his own band. I don't know whether he took it over from Snowden or not, because when I joined he had his own band.
And did Fletcher see Duke as a threat, an upcoming rival?

No, see, it wasn't so many bands in New York then, like it turned out later. Because, after that, they started coming in all directions, far and wide, far and wide. Big bands started opening up. The Dorsey Brothers hadn't come there then. Benny Goodman wasn't thought of, and Harry James wasn't thought of.
Well, a lot of big bands, they came later. And all on the strength of Fletcher having a big band. Well, naturally, some of those bands had more backing than he had, and they could make it, see.
But before you joined Henderson, were you with Shrimp Jones at the Banville, or was that after --
Shrimp Jones?
Yeah.
No, Shrimp Jones, he was a good friend of mine. He had a band at Shuffle Along, which was a show with Florence Mills. And he went to Europe with that band and came back.
But that was in 1920.
Yes, but weren't you in Shrimp's --
I wasn't in his band, no.
You were never in his band?
No, I wasn't in his band, no.
Did you ever record with Maud Mills, Florence's sister?
No, no, no. So --
So the first band you were with, other than Honey's, was Fletcher's.
That was the big band, yeah. First big band, yeah. That was my first big band.

Well, Fletcher was a very -- he was a fellow that -- he was strict and nice and exact in everything he did. But he wasn't satisfied with his band. And he threatened to fire Coleman Hawkins more than once, because Coleman used to come in late. Sometimes we'd open up and start playing, and here comes Coleman. But when he'd get up there and pick that horn up, everybody was satisfied.
But Fletcher didn't like it. But the band predomi-
nated and pleaded, please don't do it. Where are you going to get another saxophone player like him? You couldn't get another tenor in New York like Coleman. Coleman was great.
What about money? What kind of money did you make in the Henderson band?
I made sufficiently, we made sufficiently to live, more than I had been making.
Did you get extra for recording?
Oh, yes, yeah, all that was extra, sure. A lot of recordings. In this respect, I had been playing before then mostly popular music. And we had to make a lot of music that was more on the blues side.

Now, one time, when I was working with them, I played for the fellow, W.C. Handy, that wrote the St. Louis Blues. These fellows that had come out of the Army -- and they all belonged to the Amsterdam, a guy by the name of Casco Williams, the saxophone player. He and Cecil knew each other, they had been in the band together, Jim Mueller's band. And they were short a trumpet player one time, and Cecil told him, said, Casco, why don't you get Scotty? He knows all the popular tunes, he could play.

They got me, and I was scared to death. Old Man Handy was on the job. We played down on Fifth Avenue in a millionaires house, because those days, there was nothing but millionaires that owned the places there. They hadn't torn them all down
for office buildings then. We played there -- of course, they had a big palatial place, and we were situated in the corner nice, and, oh, it was grand.

Naturally, it was befitting that they play St. Louis Blues, and them being there and all like that, we'd play it. Well, I took a chorus on St. Louis Blues myself. Somebody said, take another one. I took another one. And then we played and played and played. After we got through, we -- whatever they were serving the guests to eat, the always had somebody special to serve the band, too. We were in the corner table, always got what they got, all that fancy food and stuff. And, me, I could never afford to buy what I ate.

And Old Man Handy said, Kid Scottie -- he called me Kid Scottie -- he said, I like the way you played my number. Said, you keep up the work like that and you'll go someplace. See, that hit me, that made me feel awfully good, because there he was,the author of the St. Louis Blues. And everybody did the St Louis Blues. That was the first blues they learned how to play.

Well, it looked like -- here, there and everyplace, here come another blues, another blues, another blues. And I had to make records of blues. Well, I got sick of them, because when you get down to fundamentals, the blues are nothing but the blues. And if you know one good blues solid, you can play any of them.
You were on a lot of records with different singers doing blues. It must have been very monotonous.

Yes, yes. Yes, but you know what I preferred? I preferred to play popular music. Because people seemed to like popular music. They danced better, they enjoyed it better, because they could sing and hum it. And the blues was just the blues. It's just different words and a different signature on top, that's all. But it was still the blues. So that's what it was.

And then, here the band started jumping up, too. The Dorsey Brothers and (inaudible) Benny Goodman, Guy Lombardo, he started in '28, Guy. Vincent Lopez, he started, too. And slowly but surely, each year a different band would show up. Well, they were colored bands that came to New York, too. And, of course, when they got here, I was here.

Well, you couldn't work with no more than one band at a time, because we belonged to Local 802. If you sign up for one band, you got to play with that band. You can't break your contract. But I could have played with a different band. But when I'm with one, I had to stay with one.
Well, it's a funny thing about Fletcher. Can I say something personal?
Yeah.
Fletcher married a woman that was a

trumpet player. She had played trumpet in Lafayette Theatre. They had shows, and she was in a women's band they had up there one time, a ladies' band. She played trumpet. And she had been married to a trumpet player, Russell Smith. Did you ever hear about the Smith Brothers?
(Inaudible.)

Yeah. Well, these fellows -- we used to call them -- there were three of them. And all of them came -- originally there was six of them, they came from out West someplace. But three of them got to New York. And this Russell Smith, he was a good showman and all like that, but he was no good in a dance band.

He played the shows. He played in Lou Leslie's Blackbirds one year, and other shows. Then there was Luke. Luke, he was interested in pool. He was one of the best pool players. He could beat the world's best pool shark, too. But he was a good trumpet player. But he wasn't interested in music. Then there was Joe Smith.

Now, Joe couldn't read much, but he had a nice, beautiful tone. And Fletcher's wife liked Joe, the baby. He was -- all this was trumpet, now. She and Russell Smith broke up. She married Fletcher. But Joe still hung around and all like that. She influenced Fletcher, she let Joe come in the band.
Well, I was so busy, I had never -- I had seen her

and all like that, but -- I guess she was jealous of me or something like that. But I was so busy I didn't have time to socialize much with women and all like that, although I could have, but I was too busy. I was rehearsing and making records and playing dates, and those days you were playing every night. I couldn't socialize much.

So, after we got through work, we always came to the Amsterdam, because you found out different things, what was going on with musicians. When they got off their jobs they'd come -- that was our organization, we'd come there. And that's about the (inaudible), and I did. Well, she influenced Fletcher to let Joe join the band. So Fletcher sent me a notice that after this week, my services wouldn't be required.

I took and I didn't say nothing, but it looked like -- I just sunk. I came home, and the next morning I got a phone call. Who was it but Duke Ellington. How did he hear about it so soon? See how things travel?
Yeah.

It must have been told around that he was going to change and get Joe Smith. Well, he called me, and he says, Scottie, you're open, aren't you? Well, I was open. That's what the musicians say: Are you open, and if you're open, you're open for work. You're not playing. I said, yes, Duke. He said, well, I heard you're not working with Fletcher. He says, I'd like to have you come work with me.

I didn't have the chance to feel any remorse or anything, because I went right out of the pan into the fire, so to speak. I went with him like that, the next night in the Kentucky Club. He only had one trumpet, Bubba Marley. And he had about eight pieces there, with me.

And, well, they were recording again, recording records. And you jump right into records with Duke. And we played there, and played there quite a while. You heard of Sonny Grier, he was on drums. He lives
(Inaudible) right down the street.
You know him?
Oh, very well.
And Otto Hardwick and Freddy Guy. Of course, he died, he was a guitar player. And Tricky Sam was on trombone. Yeah, he died, too. And Bro, Bro was on bass.
Yeah. Well, I guess Sonny is the only one left.
Yeah, yeah. Bro was on bass. Bro -- after he left Duke, he opened up a pool parlor and I saw him one day. I used to pass by, he'd always come out and call me, and we'd stop and talk about old times.
So then he told me one day he was giving it up, he was going back to New Orleans, his home. And I shook hands with him and wished him well. Never saw him again.
Yeah, I met his brother, I think it
was. But he spelled Braut a different way. Because Wellman spelled in B-r-a-u-x. But down there they spelled it B-r-e-a-u-x.
Oh, yeah, yeah. Yes, yes, it's a French name.
Yeah. And his brother was also -- he was playing bass down there. But -- so when you went with Duke, this was '26?
Hm?
When you left Fletcher and went with Duke --
Right away.
That was '26?
Yeah.
And how long were you with Duke?

Well, I stayed with Duke -- I'm coming to that. I stayed with Duke and we made records and records and records. And finally, Duke got a call from overseas to play at the Royal Palladium in London. And Duke told me -- and I'll tell you, Duke was a guy -- he had such a nice disposition, he was a swell fellow. And he carried himself so nicely. That's why that nickname, Duke. He got that name. His real name was Edward, but he got that nickname in Washington, D.C. That was his home. And the way he carried himself was so nice.
So when he told us about it and said we're going to leave so-and-so and so-and-so, I said to myself, now, I'm
helping my father with the family. Can I say this?
Yeah.

I'm the oldest, and after me came girls. And my mother, she was such a darling. How she made out and all like that -- my father, when he came to New York, he couldn't get any jobs. Colored men couldn't get jobs, because when the blizzard of 1888 --
Where did he come from?

Richmond, Virginia. And he was here when he was 20 years old, in 1888, he came to New York. And that blizzard so high, they didn't have the modern implements to clear a way, and it just stayed there til it melted. That's the way it was, then.

But he couldn't get any jobs outside of porters or janitor or what you call blue collar jobs. And -- but he loved horses, crazy about horses. He got a job with a white doctor, Dr. Thompson. And he drove for him, because in those days, doctors used to visit their patients. Of course, nowadays, you have to go to the doctor yourself. Doctors are scared to come out, they get mugged for dope, if they think they got dope.

But he drove the buggy for Dr. Thompson. Dr. Thompson was the doctor that brought me here. Yeah, old Dr. Thompson. And from then, he got those kind of jobs, because he didn't have a chance to get a real education, but he wanted his
children to get a good education. I was booked to be either a doctor or a lawyer, and I wound up being a musician.
How as that regarded?
Hm?
How did they take that? Was there any -- as long as you brought the money home.

Well, I was making more in four nights playing than my father made all week. And I helped the family that way, those mouths -- every time a kid would come, it was a baby girl. And he wanted another boy so bad.

Well, he finally got a boy but I was out of high school when he was born. I was playing with older men. Well, it so happened that -- I say, I was always with older men, older men. And I learned a lot from them because they had experiences over there in France and everything. I used to listen. I couldn't say anything, but I'd listen. I used to hear a lot of things. And it was an education to me in a way, because I knew how to conduct myself from their experiences.

And I always was thankful that I met a fellow like Cecil Smith. And he and I were friends to the end. There was a white local called 310 in New York City. He belonged to it, he and Casco Williams. There was just about a dozen colored fellows in the local. But then, in 1922, a new local opened up, Local 902. And they took everybody in.
Cecil told me, -- because we were working with Honey

Potter at the time, Cecil told me, -- and the trombone player, Clinton Green, to meet him the next day and he'd take us down, because he had joined. He took us down there and we joined. Two dollars to join 802. Now it costs you $75. Two dollars and they put a little sheet in front of you and say, play that. That was nothing.

And, of course, when I joined Fletcher I was with the union. We were all union men, and Fletcher and Duke and all like that. 802 right straight through. I was just going to say how good those fellows were to me, those older men. And all through my career, I was always with older men. Now, I'm on myself now, because all of them are gone.

It makes you feel kind of lonesome, because these young kids coming up, they don't appreciate music like the older ones. They were dedicated to their instruments and all like that. These young fellows just want to learn how to play the scale, and they think they know music upside down. Don't tell them nothing. Learn the scale.
And in the books at 802, there's more guitars listed than anything else. Electric guitars. Half of them don't know how to play them. But you pay $75, you can join.
You said Fletcher's wife used to play trumpet. What did people think in some days of a woman who played an instrument?
Leora, her name was Leora. What did they

think? Well, I tell you, in those days, there weren't many colored people in Harlem. And there -- a good deal of white people came there, and you had a mixed orchestra, a couple of white women was in there. And they didn't think anything, everything was all right. We didn't have any crime in those days. We fellows used to get off from work around 3:00 or something like that, we'd go by the Amsterdam or we'd go to the Rhythm Club. Because if you're working downtown, -- now, here's something.

You're working downtown, like Roseland, we got off at 1:00. We'd come up here and the Cotton Club, and don't forget Small's Paradise. Their late show was 2:00. We got in town in time to go to those shows. Well, I didn't go to the Cotton Club because, you see, some musicians didn't care for Cab because he wasn't a musician. And he took over the other fellow's job, what was his name, had the band. They just put him up on front of this band, and he was no musician.

So I had to go where the old ones went. I followed them. Come on, Scottie, you going? I say, where are you going? Well, never mind, come on, you're with me. Go this place and that place. So after we got out, anytime it'd be daylight, we'd get out of those places. And fellows have money, never nobody hold you up or nothing like that. The white fellows used to come uptown, they'd get through and they'd come by the Nest and like that. They'd cross the street, 33rd Street,

there was Mexico's, Pod's and Jerry's, private houses in the basement there, they used to have a piano. Now, you could go in there and buy a drink, because it didn't cost nothing then, and sit down, and you could play if you wanted. Piano players would come in -- those white fellows -- Benny Goodman, he was up every morning. So was Harry James, so was the fellow -- I could go on, name after name. They used to come up and jam, and jamming there, they would listen, stuff like that.

Even one time had Louis up there. He was jamming Saturday nights at Lafayette Hall. That was a big hall on the 31st Street side. And all of them used to come up, because naturally, they have a pencil, they'd take down a riff if they liked something. A little later came a new record and you'd hear that same riff.
Yes, well, didn't some bands not have the title on the music, used numbers and stuff to make it more difficult?

Yes, yes, because they stole it. So that's what they used to do. Well, sometimes I had to go with the fellows I was working with, because after all, that was the difference with musicians. You were either regular or you weren't.
Now, the regular guys, they got jobs and got work. The guys that wasn't regular they didn't bother with. So they didn't call them, they didn't get work. Had to be regular.
And regular meant -- what? What did regular mean?
They were in the clique. They called it a clique, be in the know. See, I was in the clique because I had worked with Fletcher and Duke. And then they put me in a clique, those fellows' names, see.

But if you wasn't in the clique, you didn't get that much work. You didn't get any work. You had to take what's left. The clique got the best of the jobs and what's left they got. Well, that's the way it was, that's the way it was. And it was natural.
So I think I'm a little ahead of my -- oh, no, I'm not.
Getting back to Duke, can you --
Yes, yes.
Was was on trumpet (inaudible)?
Bubba Miley.
Just Bubba Miley.

Yeah, and myself, at the time. He hadn't gotten the great big band that he has now, because I heard his son's band last year down at 12th Street, that big school, in the auditorium. Dolby, yes, he had --
(End of Side One.)
I don't mind, because I still have a long way to go.
You remember who else was in the
Duke?
Yeah. Was it Toby and Sonny?
And Sonny, the guitar player. And Braut on bass, of course, Duke on the piano. And we just had -- that was all, at that time.
Fred Guy, Sonny Grier, Braut on bass, Bubba and --
Tricky Sam was on trombone. Yeah.
Yeah, Hartwick, right?

Uh-huh. Now, we made records, started making records like that, yeah. Of course, in later years, he changed. Men died or left, like that. All the bands have to change the men, yeah, different reasons.

But, anyhow, I was telling you about going away to Europe. Well, I explained to Duke about my position. Louis Armstrong had told me, he said, Scottie, you're a city boy. You never been South, because I hadn't. He said, don't go South, because you wouldn't understand it.

He told me that. We were talking one day, like fellows do, just -- he said, don't go South because you wouldn't understand it. Well, to this day, I haven't been any further South than Richmond, Virginia. Because when I went to California, I went by the Northern route, around Cleveland and Chicago and all like that way. I haven't been South.
Because of what Louis said, or --

Yeah, well, he ought to know. He ought to know. We were good friends, because he used to write me and we used to exchange letters, even when he went to Europe. But he travelled -- when he got his own band, I lost connections with him. He couldn't keep up with travelling, and sometimes I'd be out of town myself.

And I was known around the Lafayette Theatre because I lived right across the street there at 158 West, on 31st. And the stage manager knew me. And whenever I wanted to, I could come in there and play a show because they changed shows every week, a different show.
Do you remember some of the shows?
Huh?
Do you remember some of those shows?

Well, it was the same -- it followed the same pattern all the time. They weren't like the big shows on Broadway. It just just the head man and head lady, and you had ten chorus girls, and you'd do the kickups and all like that, and they'd do their numbers, and then you'd have two comedians who'd come on, and like that.

And that's how I learned how to smoke, being in the pit, because when the comedians would come on, they were on for about ten or 15 minutes, they did their part. You'd go out of the pit and go down there and grab a smoke, see. And til

this day I don't smoke cigars, I don't smoke cigarettes. And you find very few trumpet players smoke cigars. Smoke a cigarette, but not a cigar, because most cigars -- they keep the cigar in their mouth, they're talking and all that.
Did you ever hear Bessie Smith?
Hm?
Did you ever hear Bessie Smith sing?
Yes, yes, I heard Bessie. Bessie and Ethel Waters. That was the ones that I liked the best. Oh, she was great. She was (inaudible) before then. She was great, she could sing anything.
Now, I believe you made a couple of records with Maureen.
Yeah, way back there. I think I did.
I think you were on Paramount October '24.
Yeah.
Oh, that must have been before I went with Fletcher.
Yeah.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, before I went with Fletcher.
I just want to read some of the names of people that you are believed to have recorded with.
Yeah, well, I was talking about my musical experiences in the bands. And that --
Faye Barnes. Do you remember her?
Kay Barnes?
Faye Barnes.
Faye Barnes. Singer?
Yes.
No, I don't recall.
Gladys Bryan?
Oh, I knew Gladys, yeah. Yeah, I knew Gladys.
Yeah, looks like you recorded with her.
I knew Gladys very well.
Ida Cox?
No -- I've heard of them, but I don't believe I recorded with her.
Now, you were listed as being on the very first record that Fletcher Henderson made, his very first record, with the Black Swan Company, the company that Harry Pace and --
That's right.
Now, that is July, 1921.
Yeah.
How could they get me there? I wasn't with Fletcher in '21. No, there's a mistake there someplace. '21.
'21, it says. Now, it could have been they made a mistake. It is possible it was Elmo Chambers.
It could have been. Chambers, Chambers. Chambers, he was with Fletcher before me.
I see.
Yeah.
So you didn't go with Fletcher until -- what, '23?
Yeah.
And Edna Hicks?
Uh-huh.
Rose Henderson? Now, Alberta, do you remember recording with Alberta?
She was at Lafayette, mostly, but I don't remember recording with her.
You don't remember recording with her.
No.
Viola McCoy?
You see, when I made those records, we didn't have singers. We didn't have singers, these were just musical.
But you were accompanying these singers.
Maybe there were in a different room or something. I didn't see them.
Really?
Because in those days, they made records funny. They do it different now. Each section in the band has a mike in front of it. But then you only had one mike.
And then they didn't even have a mike, they had a horn. George Williams.
Who?
George Williams.
Yeah, old George.
He's from Columbia, June 27, 1924.
Yeah.
You made a couple of things (inaudible). And who was he?
Hm?
Who was George Williams? Was he a comedian or --
He was a showman, but he wasn't no regular singer. And I can't -- those singers are so far back.
Well, of course, yeah.
And so much has happened in between, that unless you can put it right down to the very minute it's done
and recorded, it skips your mind. You have to delve in your mind and think way back then.

See, I was working what you call gigs, a lot of gigs. Work here one night, work here one night. Before I went with Fletcher, because Honey Potter, he worked mostly on the weekends. But during the week I worked gigs. So it's quite possible, but I didn't like to work with singers, record with singers. I didn't, because you had to make so many trials before you made that master, you had to go over it again and go over it again, and the singer, sometimes they were fussy, they didn't like this and that, and the band -- you knew what you were playing, but it was the singer. They didn't like this and they didn't like that, they don't like that, and, oh, boy.

(Inaudible) so fussy about it for? Why don't we get this thing over with? Then they'd have to make another one, and finally they'd say, there's the master, you'll make the master now. You make the master and that's the end of it. But you'd be there, just playing over and over and over and over again, for this old singer.
Yeah, that's true. Because experienced musicians, they knew the song. Yeah, they knew it. They knew it from A to Z. Well, anyhow, to get back to Duke.
Duke, yeah.
I talked to Duke. I talked to him, and he talked to me just like a brother. I'll never forget what he

said. He says, I'll tell you what, Scottie, I'll come up to you and speak to your mother tomorrow and explain to her about what it's all about. I says, well, I wouldn't leave her without her consent, because she was my heart.

I found out that Duke was very fond of his mother, too, in Washington, D.C. and he brought her home and everything before she died, and she died before he did, too. Well, the next morning, Duke was up there at 157 W. 123rd Street, right on 7th Avenue, that big house there. Duke showed up early in the morning. We went in the parlor and sat there, and he looked so nice. My mother told me, he's a fine-looking man. He was, too. Duke was a handsome man.

And he explained to her, an opportunity was opening up at the Gateway for me as a musician international, going over there and all like that. And he explained, and I'll never forget what she said. She said, well, Howard is agrown man now and he's able to make his own decisions. And whatever he says, I'll abide by. Right then and there, I made up my mind I wasn't going to leave her.

So I told -- when she said that, she put it on me and I was giving it to her. I told Duke -- we went to the door and Duke grabbed me by the shoulder and shook my hand, he says, Scottie, I sympathize with you. I think you made a right decision. He told me that. I never forgot him for that, boy. He was crazy about his mother. And when I said that,
he says, I think you made a right decision, patted me on the back.
Now, see, that was great.
Yeah.

That was great of him. Well, the same thing happened. I felt kind of bad that -- I felt good that Duke had told me that, and he -- I left him in a different manner that I left Fletcher. See, he shook my hand and patted me on the back. But Fletcher, I just left him.
So I felt good about it. And then, right away I went up to the musicians club. And (inaudible) had opened up the Rhythm Club around 32nd Street. You heard about that.
Yeah.
Well, that's (inaudible). I had two places to go, the Rhythm Club was nearer, and then around 130th Street was the Amsterdam. So, you see, I kept in contact with the musicians.

Well, I go around there to the Rhythm Club and I come back home, and there'd be another -- on the telephone pad there, so-and-so called up, it'd say, call them up. So-and-so called, and I'd give my sisters tips to take the calls for me. I'd give them a little money.
Well, I went around there because I was lonesome in the house. I didn't have any men to talk to. My father used to -- man, he went to work and he came home and he ate his
dinner and read the newspaper and went to bed, and he did -- that was his routine. And my brother was too small to be of any comfort to me. I had to associate with other men, fellows, see.

And that's the reason I went around and talked to the fellows. We all spoke the same language, and I went around there and they'd say, hey, did you hear, so-and-so was in town. Who? And they'd name some new musician. Where's he playing at? Well, I heard he's playing at such-and-such a place. Well, that'll circle around and everybody would go up there to hear him, to see how good he was.

That's the way it was. So I went around, and I had to pass by the Lafayette in order to get to the Rhythm Club. And Edmond Hall came walking out. And -- hello, Scottie, hey, what are you doing? I say, I'm going down to the Rhythm Club. Say, what you doing? You're with Duke, aren't you? I just left Duke. I said, well, I'm not with him right now. He said, listen, book -- I want you next week.

I'm glad I met you. They knew I could play shows. They knew I could play shows. Because I had a lot of experience. So I went in there and played a show because I wanted to circulate, and from the show I did at Lafayette right there, right around the corner was the Rhythm Club, then I'd go down to 107 W. on 30th Street, and that was the Amsterdam.
So I was in between. I kept in contact with all the
musicians. Then I went back home, because, see, when you played the shows -- then I could play other jobs, get a gig in between. And still play the show.

And, do you know, I went home and I passed by the telephone and looked, and there was -- I forget now who it was, twas a big, anyhow. Now, how did they know that I wasn't with Duke? I didn't tell them. News gets around, it got around s in those days. Anything you did, anybody else in the music world -- musicians would know about it the next day.

And so, Harry Ross was a member of the Amsterdam. Every year, we used to give a dance at -- up by the Manhatten Casino on 55th Street or the New Star Casino or some big place. And he was considered to be one of the best violinists we had. Harry Ross, did you ever hear of him?
Yeah, only from you, only that I knew you worked with him.

Well, he was going to open up at -- because he was a member of the Amsterdam, and he caught up down at the Amsterdam. I went there one night just to look around. I was still playing the Lafayette. He says, (unintelligible). Connie Simms was right by the Lafayette, but it was downstairs.
(Inaudible.)
Yeah, strictly white, no colored. Leroy Smith had been there 11 years, in Connie's Inn. So you see, he looked like he had a grip on it, and nobody -- and I never

went there and never went in there. Colored people didn't go in there, strictly white people. And I said, where you going, Connie's Inn? He say, yeah. He says, I want you to rehease with us. He named a place and he had a rehearsal band and all like that.

We went in Connie's Inn. Well, there was something different for me, too. Uptown and all, Connie's Inn, strictly white, no colored. It was nice, very nice, very nice. See, they -- Connie, he was the playboy, but George, his brother, he was the businessman. George came to us and said, listen, fellows, says, we're not going to have anybody here tonight. It's sold out to Dutch Schultze. Lord, lord, lord. (Unintelligible) I was scared to death. Dutch Schultz was the biggest gangster in town at that time.

He and his men had rented Connie's Inn. And, lord, to tell the truth, I didn't feel like I could play or nothing. I was scared to death. And I was talking to the fellow next to me, Luke Smith was working with me. Luke Smith, Luke Smith and I were good friends. He was Joe Smith's brother. Luke could play better trumpet than any of the other two. He was the best. But you wouldn't think he did it, because he liked to play pool so much.
Luke was in __________ band, Luke and I were great friends. Luke says, I ain't paying him any mind. I said, why? He says, well, they treat you nice. It'll be all right.

Then George came up to us before -- when we came in that night -- they told us the night before what was going to happen. And we came to work regularly at the same time. He comes up and says, well, fellows. just play whatever they want you to play. They'll treat you nice and all. It so happened that they went downtown, these fellows, his henchmen and all his gang or whatever Dutch Schultz had, and hired girls from -- what's that, the New Amsterdam Theatre there, 42nd Street. Had the most beautiful showgirls in the world.
It wasn't the Apollo Theatre.
Hm?
The Apollo on 42nd?
No, 42nd Street, downtown.
Yeah.
Yeah, the Amsterdam Theatre.
A white place.
Hm?
A white place.

Yeah. These girls -- well, it'll come to me. You know, you've heard of it. They hired these girls to be their companions. Paid them $100 a night. And here they come, and they're the most beautiful showgirls in the world. Now, what was that place (inaudible)?
They came -- anyhow, they came pouring in. They got their cars parked out there, big cars, Cadillacs and things.

So I heard, because other people had seen them, and even from where I lived, my folks could see these big cars out there. And they came in, and Alley -- he was the past grand master of that. He could cater to anybody, he knew just how to do it. And one of them would come in, they'd be dancing and we'd start playing and all like this.

And right away, before we had played hardly any time, the waiter came around with a tray for drinks. Drinks for us? One of the gang -- and I thought they'd all be guys with great big guns on them and everything. I had never been around any gangsters. They dressed like gentlemen. Of course, they had guns. I managed to see one gun one time, dancing around. He had it down in here.

There was guns there, but they acted like gentlemen. And tip? Oh, boy, did they tip. They come up to the bandstand and say, are you the leader? And I'd say, yes, I'm the leader, can I please you, anything you'd like? And, yes, do you mind playing such-and-such? Why, certainly. Okay, fellows, such-and-such a number, one, two, three, boom, and we knew it all and hit it just like that.

Guy would reach in his pocker and pull out a great big wad like that. (Unintelligible) to play that number. Sometimes it was 20, sometimes it was ten. And we had a kitty, had a box. Here's another one, fellows. We played all night long, because they hired the place, they could stay as late as
they pleased. And we didn't mind because we were getting tips. We were working, but those were tips. Lord, lord, lord.

When we got through that night, those guys -- every one of them had plenty of money. And there must have been 40, 50 of them. And they had plenty of money, they had plenty of girls. And they were dancing around, and liquor was flowing, and nice, wasn't any disturbance or anything. Everybody was laughing. And I thought to myself, now, all the time I've been reading about gangsters in books and things, and shooting and killing and everything. And I thought something was going to happen down there. They'd shoot somebody.

No, nothing like that. It was just nice as could be, just as nice, just as nice. And after it was all over, we counted up, and we had 11 men in the band, and each one of us got $200. Now, ain't that something?
That was a lot of money then?
I never made that many tips before in my life. Dutch Schultz. I had a $50 tip one time. The fellow didn't know it. __________ didn't know it, either.
Did Alley Ross one time conduct the Henderson band?
You see how liberal they were, good sports. I thought gangsters was just gangsters. All they'd do is shoot you and rob you. I had never come in contact with them.
Or kill each other.

Yeah. But they were just the opposite. So -- well, see, bands have commitments. (Unintelligible) the services aren't needed. We played our commitment there. Then Alley got the call for another edition of Blue Leslie's Blackbirds, downtown.

Well, we had the men that could play it. And they were all experienced showmen, had experience playing shows. Alley took the same band down there, and we played that whole time, for the show. We played the whole edition there, Leslie's Blackbirds. The last one they had, that was in 1928.
Oh, yes. That was famous.

And it was good to be back on Broadway again, because I'd been down there with Fletcher and Duke and then there was different places to go around and renew old acquaintenances and like that, because those white fellows that played down that way, you're going to meet them down that way. And they used to come up to Harlem and meet them down there, and one time, I was with a couple of guys and we went in Lindy's. And no colored people went into Lindy's.

I says, hey, wait a minute, fellows. Come on, we're going to get a little bite in here. I said, that's Lindy's, isn't it? Gee, that's a ________ place, all the show people went in there. Of course, we all had tuxedos on. We lived in tuxedos all the time. You're with us, Scottie, come on. (Inaudible) never mind, we can go down the street there at the

automat and get something. No, no, come on in. Well, the four of us went in, we sat at a table, and I was served. And that's the way it's been with me most of my life. Now, I didn't come in contact with any discrimination that they talk about and all like that. I didn't experience any of it, because when I was born in New York, -- we all lived downtown. When I was born, there was no colored people in Harlem at all. None at all. And what few there were lived downtown, and gradually, around 1910, Coleman Johnson was a team in vaudeville. They bought a apartment on 135th Street, between Fifth and Lennox.

Well, they were decent respectable people that moved in there. And gradually, a house opened here and there and there, and finally, we came to Harlem. And when we got there, everybody on the block knew everybody else, white or colored. Because across the street from us was all white. It was four colored people on our block, four houses, I mean. We visited each other, yeah. The women knew each other, visiting and all like that.

So I didn't know all this -- what they talk about now, that discrimination stuff. I didn't experience -- because I was a professional man, and in the professional business, there's no discrimination. We don't have that. So we finished the show down there, and of course, I was a little older then. And I could get around more than when I was with Honey Potter.

And I associated and I met plenty of people, and there was Ed Small. He was boss of -- he owned Small's Paradise. Charlie Johnson was in there, had the band for years. Charlie and I became very good friends. I used to go in there, and one time there was a showgirl that I took up there once, and some gangster up there, Jerry Preston, he was after her or something like that. And somebody said that she was in there, going to Small's Paradise with Scottie, the trumpet player. We just went in there one night, there was a bunch of us together, from the show.

And Jerry made a remark that I'm coming after him. And it came to me. And Ed Small heard about it. He's the boss. Well, he sent word to me that -- come on in there whenever you want, Scottie, Jerry ain't coming after anybody. And I knew all the fellows in the band, in Charlie Johnson's band. And I could have played in his band, but I was working.
And we became very good friends.
Charlie had a good band.
Oh, he had a good band. Yeah, he had a good band. Most of those guys are gone, too. I went to their funerals. Lord, I've been to more funerals of musicians. So many, so many.
Well, anyway, Alley Ross did the show. Well, the show ended. I come back uptown, naturally, and go down, gigging, and I played -- I didn't lose any time because I

worked the very next night and the very next night, kept on working. And one fellow wanted me to come down to the Elks with him. Something happened around there, I don't know. Said, oh, come on, -- you know how you go with fellows, just meet them, come on and have a couple of drinks.

We went down there, and the guy wanted me to put a band in there. I told him I -- he said, oh, this is just for Sundays, a couple of hours. We need some music and all like that. So they finally convinced me. No music, didn't need any. The fellows I chose knew everything. They knew everything. And I had five men in there, and we just played regular dixieland stuff, like that.

Ed Small called me, too, and told me every Sunday he wanted me to come in there with Dixie. Now, that meant that I worked twice on Sundays, afternoon and night. Well, when you keep that up, gradually -- of course, I was at home, getting my meals there, but gradually it'll tell on you later on. You can't feel it, you don't realize it, because you're happy, carefree.

And I had a pocketful of money and I had put a little money in the bank, and the family was living comfortably and I was happy. All right, here come a call from Chick Webb, opening up at the Savoy. No, no, I'm ahead of myself. Fats Waller, Fats Waller, in between, called me. Come to the Capital. Well, I had been visiting there, because when the place opened,

and you get from work and you see the musicians in the band and you hear them, and nobody bothered you then. You wasn't held up or nothing in the streets. Everybody could walk along the streets any time of night, just carefree.

And I'd been there and all like that, and I was acquainted with Fats, and he wanted me to come in on the band for awhile. I did, I did about three or four weeks down there with him, but I didn't like the downstairs. I was more used to Broadway, I didn't like working up there. This was different from Connie's Inn, Connie's Inn was sedate and all like that, and the Capital was a little more honkytonk and stuff.
I didn't care for it, so I got away from it. But I liked Fats, he was great. You know, that guy, they had to put a new piano in there about every two or three months, he was so heavy-handed.
Oh, really?
Yeah. But he could play, though, and entertain. Fats Waller was great, he was great, he was great.
What year was this, when you were called by Fats?
Oh, this was between -- right after I came out with Alley and -- '29 and '30, yeah. '29 and '30, yeah. That was before the Savoy opened up.
Well, I was getting more situated as far as -- I was known, and I knew -- I wasn't scuffling, you might say,
because I had made money and had a little bank account. And I was more or less secure and felt more secure, and I didn't mind working.

Now, in between, -- oh, yeah, Chick wanted me, and so I felt sorry for Chick, he was handicapped. He's a good little drummer, but he was handicapped. And he was trying to get a band together. And he talked so nice, he pleaded with me. And I didn't know, so I said no. But news travels around. So I went in with him. And you know who was in the band? Johnny Hodges.
Oh.

Johnny Hodges was in the band before he went with Duke. He was in that band. He and Elmer Williams on sax. And Slats Slattery, Johnny Truehart was on guitar, Slats was on trombone, with me and Louis Bacon. And Chick on the drums. And Kirkpatrick was on piano, yeah, Kirk. Nice little band.

And then the Savoy was nice, just opened, nice, nice, Of course, I left there before it got rough and rowdy. Still Sundays, I had that little band down at Ed Small's. See, those men -- we didn't need any music, they knew everything. And my inspiration had been from -- maybe -- there was a band out in Memphis called the Memphis Five. Years and years ago.
Joe Napoleon?
Huh?
he means Phil
Joe Napoleon?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. They made records. Of course, I'm in New York, but I got their records. I like their style, Dixieland.

So I -- of course, I wasn't exactly stealing. But I liked the style they played. And I played that style down at Small's and they all went crazy about it. They went crazy about it. Strictly Dixieland. Yeah, because I'm not that type of player. Now, you know who stole from me? Harry James. He used to come up there and listen to me playing and all like that. I played on that style. Establish the tune and all like that, and then I'd improvise on my trumpet. As I felt, and that's the way he played.

But his father was a very rich man. And his father just put out money and got him a good agent, put him in, and the first thing you know, he's on Broadway. That money -- money talks. So he used to come up there. Yeah, Harry stole my stuff.

Well, I didn't mind, because after all, that's what -- the fellows were going around, everybody was stealing -- the new trumpet players were trying to steal Louis' stuff, Louis Armstrong. And you used to see more trumpet players, they used to sing, sometimes, and had a little patch over their lip. Say, what's the matter with you, fellow? What you do, hit yourself? Cut your lip? Oh, no, man, I was just practicing.
Come to find out they were trying to hit those high notes like Louis used to hit.
Oh, yeah, that's right.

And Louis hit them with ease. They were trying to squeeze them out. They'd split their lips and everything like that. I never believed in that. I believe, be yourself and be natural and you're much better appreciated. See, and Louis was natural. You can't beat that, originality in anything, because anything that comes along is just a copy of the original. It's imitation. But the original thing you can't beat. Like the soda, Coca-Cola. When I was a little tiny kid, I used to drink it. Still going strong. And you got Pepsi-Cola and you got this and you got all kinds of different kinds of sodas. Imitation. But Coca-Cola is the original.
You didn't mention at all about Johnny Dunn.

Yeah, old Johnny Dunn. I knew Johnny, a trumpet player, yeah. He was a tall fellow, brown skin, and nice looking. He was in -- oh, what's the name of that show? Hot Chocolates. Yeah, Hot Chocolates. He was in that show, yeah.
Yeah, he was very popular, wasn't he?
But he didn't last long. He didn't last long. Johnny -- yeah, he came up and he was popping that

show, but after that you didn't hear much of Johnny. And the first thing I know, he just disappeared. And we didn't know where he went. And somebody said he died, but it wasn't verified, I don't know.
Well, I know he went to Europe for awhile.
Yeah, he went to Europe, and he just lost contact with the main guys and all like that. Johnny Dunn was a nice trumpet player, years ago, yeah. So, I left Chick and here comes -- where was I?
You went with Chick, you joined Chick then.

Yeah, yeah. Well, I stayed with him awhile. But all the time, I was getting off and coming in there and all like that, sometimes it was really annoying, because you can't break a contract when you're playing with one and the other, and this guy wants you to play so-and-so, and you can't do it. I couldn't do it. It really used to get on my nerves, sometimes. Sometimes I'd have two gigs a night, and I'd go around the Rhythm Club and I'd find a trumpet player that wasn't working that night. Call up the guy and tell him I couldn't make it but I'm sending a good guy in my place. And they couldn't say anything about it. But, you
know what I mean? You couldn't work all that -- it was too much work. How could I work two places? The union wouldn't allow it, and how could I possibly do it?

So Lucky Roberts, he called me up and asked me, could I play some dates with him. Well, I'd heard of him. Lucky played for strictly rich people. Well, I had played for rich people on Fifth Avenue, because nothing but rich people used to live there. I played for rich people. But he had rich people out in Westbury and around there, and around Southampton, where the rich people used to be living at one time. Not now, but then. Nothing but rich people -- the Goulds, the Vanderbilts, the Astors, the Rockefellers and all the rich people.

Well, he asked me, did I have any open dates? I told him I'd look and see. I was working at the time, but he said, I'd like to have you play with me, Scottie, let me know. So I went to my good old friend -- Cecil Smith wasn't playing then, he wasn't playing, he'd given it up. He was keeping a bar near the Amsterdam.

And he was the one that advised me to go with Fletcher. And I listened to him because he was older and more experienced than me, and he knew more about Lucky Roberts than I did. So I told him about it, and he said, well, I'll tell you like I told you about Fletcher. He says, there's good money in it, those rich people pay good money. Said, if Lucky

called you and he's got an open gig, take it. The only thing is, he doesn't pay you right away, because those rich people, they pay by check. Like the other places, you get your money when you get through. No.

Well, I didn't mind that because I was working and I had a little money myself. He said, well, when you get an open date, then call. So I called him. Lucky, he says, oh, I'm glad, Scottie, you're just in time. And he gave me a gig. And it was for rich people, out there in Westbury.
This is after you left Chick Webb?
Yeah.
What year? Do you remember what year?
Oh, this was '31.

Now, see, from then on I'm not working a long time with anybody because things were beginning to change then. And I wanted to travel. I wanted to see some of the United States. I hadn't seen it. I'd been to just Washington, D.C., around the horn, that's Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington, with the show. And I hadn't seen anything out West.

Well, I played some gigs with Lucky Roberts, yeah. Nice, nice, very nice. And then the same Talley Johnson called me one night and says, Scottie, when you get off there, stop by, I want to tell you something. Well, after I got through

work, I went by and he told me, there's a new band in town, Alex Jackson, from Cincinnati, Ohio. And he said, I had a commitment to play in Detroit, but I'm anchored here with Ed Small and I have a contract I have to-- and I know this guy, Jackson, he's a nice fellow.

And you said you'd never been out West. Here's a good chance for you to do it. I'll tell him about you. Alex Jackson. Well, he was a nice handsome man. I said, well, why not, to myself. And Charlie said, well, Scottie, here's your chance.

Well, he formed the band. We opened up in Detroit. Now, this is '32. Opened up in Detroit. Grand Boulevard and Joy Road, the Mirror Ballroom. And we stayed there six months. And I lived in Detroit, and I found -- that's Motor City, and (unintelligible) for almost nothing. $100, and I got a car. Well, it was a used car, but just to get around.

That was nice, very nice. We came back, then we came to this home town. Then he wanted to go out West. He had been booked. So we went to Chicago, Cleveland, Chicago and all that, and then finally, California. And we were booked ahead. Well, I don't got a whole lot of experience -- at the same time, I was sending money back home. And my mother, she was saving it for me. Can you beat that?
What a woman. And that's how -- I wanted to see the Golden Gate of San Francisco.
