So you were saying where you came home from San Francisco.
Yeah, I --
When you went to Chicago and San Francisco, did you hear any music that you remember that particularly impressed you?

I worked a couple of gigs in Chicago, but (unintelligible) in the union. You go around and you meet musicians wherever you go. Because they can coach you and steer you around. It was strange for me, in those cities. I'd never been there before. But when you meet musicians and they know you -- and they had heard of us. They hear about you, you'd be surprised. If I was out West I'd know about fellows in New York.
And I liked it, it was an experience for me. And I was playing with Alex Jackson's band. And -- one nighters.
What did Alex Jackson play?
Sax, he was a saxophone player.
You had stopped making records?
We made records. We made records with Alex Jackson. We made records -- yeah, we made records in Detroit, and we made a couple in Chicago, yeah. Yeah, we made records.
One record I didn't like at all, because -- I told you

about the blues, this was called the Crazy Horse Blues. I was so disgusted with that that I had to (inaudible). It was nothing but the same blues that you hear everyplace, everywhere, but it was just a different name. It was a different record company out there, so -- Crazy Horse Blues. That's one of the records I remember.
We took up at 1931 when you came back from the tour.
No, this was '32, going to '33.
No, somewhere during that period, didn't you go with Benny ?

No, I knew Benny, but I didn't work with him,no. See, I was working at the time. I knew Benny, I remember one time when I was coming from the Amsterdam or something. And Gene and I, we were walking down the avenue and we met Benny. And he seemed kind of disconsolate. I asked him what was the matter, and he said, oh, Scottie, I'm kind of disgusted, I'm going to leave New York.

And there he is, a good saxophone player like he was. I said, what, leave? Why, Benny? He says, I don't know, it looks like I just can't get anywhere and all like that. I don't know, and he'd been playing and writing and making records and things. So we were going down to an opening, Jack Fuller was opening up his place, at the old Colony, and he was opening that night. And we were going by there, and I say, come

on with us, Benny. We took him down there, and we sat there, the three of us. And we had a couple of drinks. And I tried to convince him, but his mind was made up. He says, I'm going out to California.
(Inaudible.) And it listed you as being in the band, and they raised the question, they wanted to know if Benny Carter was stealing the Henderson band. You don't remember anything about that?

No, well, see, that was after I left Fletcher. That was after I left Fletcher. But, see, I went straight with Duke, then. And I didn't go with Bennie, no. Bennie didn't make good with bands here. But he went out to Chicago -- California, out there, and tore up California. He made gangs of records out there. They had bands out there -- there's nothing but Benny Carter out there now.
Okay. So you were saying -- did we -- you were saying that you were reminded of some other things you can done.
Yes.
Does that cover that period we were talking about?

Well, this is after what we were talking about. This is -- that was J.P. Johnson mentioned in that __________, and I was kind of confused. But here it was. He wrote a show and the name of the show was Lazy Rhythm, in
James P. Johnson, yeah.

Yeah. And Lyle had connections with that show, too. Benny Heath and I were in that show, and it was over in Brooklyn, at the Banks Theatre, I think. Yeah, Banks Street Theatre. But it only lasted one week. And then, of course, we were working odd jobs here and there.

Then we went to Mac Dean's. That was on Jerome Avenue. This was in '35. Now, the show was in late '34, and in '35 we started -- for three seasons we were at Maxine's. And that was a supper club up on Jerome Avenue.
What kind of club was it?

A regular -- a nightclub. And they had a lot of celebrities. Jimmy Durante, the nose, he was one of them. And Evelyn Nesbeth, you don't remember her because she was connected with Harry K. way back there, in that big scandal that time. They had a -- but she was an old-timer. She came there, one of the acts. Very difficult to play for, because she'd stop in the middle of the singing, and see somebody at a table she knew, she'd start talking to them. And then you'd wait til see got through, and then she'd pick up and the band had to grab where she left off at.
Very difficult. But she was very nice, though.
Can you tell me more about that show?
Oh, the James P. Johnson show had a

-- well, we had to work with a group of people in there. I don't remember them all now, but -- because I played so many shows. They had the regular setup -- showgirls and the comedians and I really don't remember who they were, I'll tell you the truth.

All I remember is that it didn't last long, and we were so upset. I got my money, and whoever told us it was going to be a long run -- yeah, one week. Didn't have the correct backing. Now, Maxine's was a different place. Very nice. And when that closed, Maxine's closed, we went to City Island, at the Showboat, it was a place in City Island that we went to.

And McGuire was the name of the boss there, McGuire. And we played there for about -- oh, two or three months, I think. Yeah. That was nice. We used to drive out there every night. Now, during that time, television was beginning to sneak in, only rich people had it at that time because -- and the big bands, one by one, was starting to wake up, and nightclubs were starting to fold up. Because during that era when television came in, everything went out, all that live music.
You're now talking about the '40s.
Yeah, the late '40s, yeah.
Before you do that, what happened in (inaudible).

Well, (inaudible) the '40s now. The United States went to war, war broke out. Well, the fellows weren't doing very much work, and those fellows that had quit from the big bands, they were all getting jobs downtown as messengers. One musician worked at a chemical bank, and he had -- what do you call it, bookings for the rest of the musicians at other banks. And he got them in the banks.

Because they weren't working, they had to raise their families, had to make money somehow. And they weren't working, so they got jobs that way, or a very lot of them, a whole lot of them. And I got a call, again, from the government, because I was on the Civil Service list, for Sperry Gyroscope. It's in Long Island City. This is right there, because a lot of those fellows were taken into the Army. And so they replaced them with Civil Service men.
So I stayed there all during the war. Now, I only worked the five days. On Saturdays and Sundays I had my playing jobs.
What did you do at Sperry Gyroscope?

Oh, I was just -- like, an assistant electrician, like that, because I'm not an electrician by any means. But I assisted the regular ones. We had that sort of work to do, like carpenter work and all like that, and filing and so forth. And I had regular tools. It wasn't hard or difficult. For being a musician, I really liked that for a
change. I was learning something, yeah. They make gyroscopes, that they put on big ships, that steer them.
Right.
Yeah.
But you were still performing.
I'm still a musician, sure. I worked every night. Every Saturday night I had a job, a gig, and every Sunday night. And I worked five nights there.

I meant to ask you, going back now to the Henderson band, there seems to be a lot of confusion in a lot of the systems whether the first playing is you or Elmer Chambers. Were your styles that similar?
About Elmer Chambers and me?
Yeah.
Well, all the records I played, Elmer Chambers was there, yeah.
But there are some record collectors who--
Well, after I left, Elmer Chambers played with another man.
Yeah.
That's all.
There's some confusion on some of the records whether it was you playing or whether it was Elmer playing.
Yeah.
So what I'm saying, were your styles that different or could you mistake one for the other?
No. Ain't no chance of that.
No. What was basically the difference?

Well, our styles was different. Elmer played first trumpet, I played second and I took solos. Yeah. And he stuck strictly to first trumpet. That's all he does, he was the momentum of the band in the brass section. Sure, he has to carry the brass section. He doesn't play all that hot stuff and all like that. He's the main one in the brass section.
If you were to name a musician, trumpet player or other musician, who influenced you the most, who would you --

Who influenced me the most? Well, the one that I got most influence from was Louis, Louis Armstrong. Because Louis and I got very close. And he style was so different and everybody would listen to him. I didn't try to imitate him because nobody can do Louis. He was just Louis and that was all.

But he told me about a lot of different things out West and all like that, and wasn't any particular trumpet player around at that time that -- Henry Busse, he worked with -- I knew him with Paul Whitman. He was Whitman's trumpet player. And then Red Nichols came along at that time, and he
worked at Roseland, he was a nice trumpet player. You know Red Nichols and his Five Pennies? They made a lot of records. I liked them both.
And then you also -- you didn't work with Bubba Miley.
Bubba Miley?
Yeah.
I certainly did.
No, Bubba used a lot of mutes, a lot of effects.

Yeah, but Bubba wasn't like these other guys. Well, he wasn't as advanced as these other fellows. He was all right, because he didn't stay with Duke very long. Duke started with him. He was the fellow that could play first, and then he took a little jazz and so forth. He was the wow-wow mute and all like that.
Are you saying, did he not have good techniques?
Well, now, I don't think he did, no. No, he didn't. He wasn't that far advanced on the trumpet.
But he could growl.

Oh, he could do all that, yeah. Yes, he could grow. That was the name I was trying to think of, growling. He could do a lot of growling, he's expert at that. Did a lot of growling. But there comes a time when they put
Couldn't read much.

No, he wasn't that advanced. He wasn't that advanced. And sometimes, a fellow -- somebody come up with a manuscript and hand it around and (unintelligible). And (unintelligible) or whoever it was just wanted to get an idea of what the men could do, see. He knows what it's supposed to sound like, but he wants to see which one could read good and which one couldn't.

So, all right, fellows, let's go now, start from the top, left, right, lefthand corner, all right. And if you can read what's on there, you'd go straight ahead and read it until he tells you to stop. But when he tells you to stop, he's got a pretty good idea who's reading their part and who isn't.

And then again, some guys would give you that and say, well, we're going to go until you get it right. And you keep on practicing and practicing and practicing. Those guys who couldn't read so good had a chance to get it down underneath their skulls, what it was supposed to be. But it takes time, see. And then they learn about who could read and who couldn't.
Well, I could read and that's -- Allie Ross told me once (inaudible) because he wanted to know why he always hired

me. Well, Allie says, well, I'll tell you one thing. He's a nice trumpet player, but he says, when I put that manuscript down there, I want to hear what's on that manuscript. Scotty can read, but you can't read like Scotty.
Did you ever have -- come into contact with the gangster element?
I beg your pardon?
You told me about the Dutch Schultz, the time Dutch Schultz played --

Oh, yeah, well, he wasn't there himself. That was his -- the Ziefeld Follies, that's what it was. Yeah, yeah, the Ziegfeld Follies. It came to me as I left and was on the bus. I said, oh, lord, why couldn't I remember.
The night at Connie's Inn, when Dutch was there, the girls they had rented were all from the Ziegfeld Follies.

Yeah, because the theatres let out at 11:00. And, see, the nightclubs -- they had rented the place, they came in there afterwards. We just waited for them to come in. When they came in, they had these girls. And they had hired them. I don't know what they paid them, but I know they'd paid plenty of money.
Well, Elmer told me on a couple of occasions that they used to -- because you used to play, I think, baritone sax, bass sax, a lot of heavy instruments, they used

to leave them in the club. And on a couple of occasions, the boss said, take your instruments home tonight. And the first time he didn't do it, and the next morning the place was burned down. So the second time he did it, and sure enough, the place was burned down.
At what club was that?
I think he was talking about the Kentucky Club.
Oh, the Kentucky Club. Yes, well, we were in there and he came in afterwards.
But what I'm saying, do you ever recall anything like that? Where the club was seriously burned?
No, not in my experience, no. I don't remember anything. Not where I was working. No, they didn't burn it down like that.
Now, you didn't really get much in the way of tips being in a big band. The singer might get a tip or the band leader, for being just up there. In the trumpet section, the tips were not --
Why didn't we get tips?
Hm?
Why didn't we get tips?
Or did you? I'm asking you.
Certainly. Well, see, they'd give the tips to the leader.
Oh, then you'd split it.
Then we'd split it. I told you that.
That's right.
Sure we'd get tips.
Did that amount to much?

Yeah, well, when Dutch Schultz was there we got $200 apiece. That was just tips that night. Those guys -- and when they came around and asked Alley -- of course, we knew everything they'd call popular songs. We knew all them. Do you know so-and-so? Alley would say, certainly, and we'd play for them.

Yeah, and he didn't look to see what he was giving you. It might be a five or a ten, just like that. Alley would show it to us and say, well, here, fellows. It'd be a 20, there, and put it in the box. And we'd be playing til they came around again and asked for something, then we got some more.

Oh, we entertained them. They liked the music and everything they asked us to do, we did. So they paid us well for it. But I was scared to death, though. I was scared they would get to fighting down there, and maybe shoot me. Who knew?
Do you remember any of the women who were in Mrs. Henderson's band, when she had her all-girl orchestra?
Marie Lucas was one.
What did she play?
Yeah, and the rest of them, I didn't -- I was very busy at that time.
Yeah. What did Marie Lucas play?

She played piano, and I think she played a little violin, too. But I never worked with any women except Sinto. She was a violinist, but she had all men. I never worked with any women. There weren't many women orchestras at that time, no.
Do you remember (inaudible)?
Yeah, I remember them, but I never worked with them.
Never heard of them?
I've heard of them. Bessie Smith, all those --
No, no, did you ever hear (inaudible) play trumpet?

No, I don't believe I did. If I did, it was on a record. You see, when I came along, it was mostly men. The women hadn't become prominent then. And -- of course, later on they had girls' bands and all like that, but I didn't come in contact, no.
(Inaudible.)
The women were in the background then. They hadn't -- they had women's suffrage at that time, they
hadn't begun to vote, when I started. Yeah.
We got to talking about the Benny Carter band. Now, what happened after -- was it right after the Benny Carter band that you went to James Johnston show or --

That was -- we were talking about Benny Carter. It was around that time. Something had happened, and I couldn't remember what it was, but this is what happened. This came after that, after I started with Benny. It came after that, yeah.

Then after the war was over, Harry Truman was President. That was cool, because the other guys came back. Well, then, that was the height of what you'd call the Depression or whatever it was, there weren't any big bands, the shows were closing, the big shows, the Capitol, the Strand, Broadway. Of course, the Paramount, that was still going.
And up in Harlem, everyplace was closing (inaudible), everyplace was closing. So there wasn't much work to be done. But there was a fellow that was getting jobs. You ever hear of Fess Finley?
Fess Finley?
Yeah.
No.
No? Well, in those years, he was a band leader, he had charge of the Manhattan Elks band. But he used to get a lot of work around that time. He was the big one,
because the others had to close up and go on and all like that. He liked me and I liked him, too. He was a trumpet player, a good trumpet player, too.

So I did work with him. That's who I was working with when I got the call to go in the post office. I was working with Fess. Fess had an average of about three or four jobs a week. And it was remarkable at that time, because nobody was working in music. Things were closed up in town. Oh, it was a terrible time.
When was the last time you made a record? Or appeared on a record?
Well, the last that I can recall was Alex Jackson. In Alex Jackson's band. Because I'd (unintelligible) before them, but after that there wasn't any -- I wasn't with the record-making --
Uh-huh. So that's been a very long time, that you haven't made a record.

That's right. I wasn't particular about it, because it happened -- most singing and like that, to tell you the truth, what I like about bands, I like to hear a band play. I like that music. I like it because in my mind, I could hear the different sections. And I liked to hear what each section was playing and all like that. Walk in the street and still hear that song in my mind.
It's a funny thing. And I would go home, and I used
to take my pen and write down the position of each man on the band, and how he was sitting, and just look at it like that, then I could hear that number they played.
Well, see, it was all music with me. Singers came in there and it did something to the music. I don't know. The band had to stop and the singers had to come in there and (unintelligible).
Did you ever write songs?
Me? No, I wasn't a writer. I liked to play them, I loved to play. I didn't go in for writing myself, no. Let me play. I want to play. That's all I wanted to do.
Now, what about after the war, when bebop came in? How did that sound to you?

Bebop -- listen, real musicians didn't like any bebop. They didn't like bebop. They didn't like it, that's all there is to it. They didn't like it. And right now, it's so nice with the big bands coming back in again, because it was nothing but a gang of noise, repetition, repetition, repetition, repetition.
Where is the music? There's no music.
What about someone like Dizzy Gillespie?
Dizzy dances?
No, Dizzy Gillespie.
He's just what you were saying -- dizzy. That's what we called him then. He's crazy. He's crazy.
You didn't like anything he played?
Listen, he had a good band at one time, but I'm talking about the man himself. He still is kind of off up there. He always was. That's not his real name, but we nicknamed him that, Dizzy. Yeah.
But he was playing with Frankie Fairfax, he was playing with Cab Calloway. He was playing with regular bands.
Yes, yes, yes.
At one time, he was sounding exactly like Roy Eldridge.

Well, see, he's so dizzy, he tries to play everybody. What did Dizzy do, trying to be like Roy Eldridge? He was a doggone good trumpet player, and Roy came along and at the time they needed somebody like him, because Louis had gone on his own, with his own band, travelling all over the world.
And Roy came along at a time when they needed somebody just like him. He was good, too. And Rex Stuart, he was a good trumpet player.
Yeah.
Those men fit in just at a time when they needed them. They needed men like that.
What about today, when you hear someone like Oscar Petersen? Is that too far out for you?
Oscar Petersen?
Yeah.
I don't know. When did you hear him last?
Last week.
Last week?

Probably, yeah. I'm just wondering -- I know that bebop when it first came out, it was kind of startling to a lot of people who were not used to it. But as the years have gone by, and this other music has appeared that sounds even farther out --
Yeah.
-- bebop begins to sound a little normal, doesn't it?
Yeah, well, see, it took to the younger people. They came up with bebop, yeah.
Right.
And they liked it more. But the fellows my age and all like that, they didn't like it. They didn't like it.
Well, have you changed your mind at all about bebop or modern jazz?
No, because -- you know why? The modern bands are coming back. Now, last night they had Lawrence Welk. Did you hear him on Channel Five?
No.

I told you to get him. Yeah. He featured the band, two members in the band, his trombone player, one of his saxes, his clarinetist. He has a big band, and they're playing modern music now. When he first started, he had that champagne style of music, and I didn't like it.

But just like the fellow said up at the Amsterdam, he heard Lawrence Welk, he said, gosh, he's really got it bad now. They sounded great. Four trumpets, four trombones, he had five saxes, three violins, a cello, a bass drum and guitar. That was a solid band. And they played, too. They were very good. I was listening to them all by myself. And I said to myself, I hope oldtime musicians are listening to this.
When was the last time you played (inaudible)?

Well, the last time I remember playing is -- by myself, I was trying out my lip after I came out of the post office, (unintelligible). See, I was hurt in the post office. When I came to, I was at the medical center, and it looked like about six doctors around me. It was only two.
What happened?
I fell out. But they had done everything I reckon because (unintelligible), what I had been doing there, my constitution was just worn down, and I needed rest.
You were in the post office when, from
1951 -- is that when you started?
'52 until what time?
Until '54. Yeah.
And what have you done since?

Well, there wasn't -- I couldn't go anywhere, I was a sick man. I was a sick man. And I told you, I went to specialist after specialist, and all I money went for doctors' medicine, doctors' -- there was that one man who said he could cure me, he was a homeopathic doctor. And he did me a lot of good, and he told me, well, he got one arm up so I could raise it. He was working on this one when he died.

Now, the kind of medicine he gave me, I do not know what it was. It was his own, he got his own medicine. But had he lived, he would have cured me entirely. He said he would. He said, it'll take time, Scotty. It'll take time. You got to do exactly like I want. He was a good man, too, and when you have faith in your doctor, you can heal with him, because you work with your doctor. If you don't like your doctor, there ain't no sense going to him, because you're not going to get well.

He was very nice to me and I liked him. He used to take me around with him to visit. I'd be going along the avenue sometimes and I'd hear somebody -- hey, Scottie, I'd look around and hear, come here, come here. (Unintelligible.)
I'd say, Doctor, I got to go on and (unintelligible), and he'd say, never mind that, tell them you're with me. Come on, I want to show you something.
